newsitem.title: CANADA: Ontario Hydro takes charge, operation cutbacks.
newsitem.headline: Ontario Hydro takes charge, operation cutbacks.

text.p: Ontario Hydro, North America's biggest power utility, said on Tuesday that it would take a C$2.5 billion charge against 1996 income to strengthen its financial structure.

The debt-laden Ontario government-owned utility said that its board also approved a C$600 million charge against 1997 earnings. The charges were related to operating decisions and changes in accounting policies.
As a result, Ontario Hydro estimated its 1996 net loss at C$1.9 billion. The utility previously forecast net income of C$600 to C$625 million.

"These decisions are driven by our determination to improve nuclear performance and to make capital and policy decisions that enable us to succeed in the business environment we face," said Ontario Hydro president and chief executive officer Allan Kupcis.

He said the decisions will not impact the utility's cash flow, borrowing requirements or debt outstanding. They also will not affect Hydro's ability to pay down its debt, estimated at over C$30 billion.
Among its operating moves, the utility said it will not proceed with retubing Unit I at the Bruce A Nuclear Station.
"Hydro's surplus generating capacity and the higher than planned production costs for nuclear are contributing factors for this decision," said Kupcis.

He said the retubing decision, which resulted in a writedown of C$250 million, could be reviewed if demand increased and the costs compared favourably with other options. Hydro said it would continue to rely on electricity from Bruce Unit 1 until the unit was laid up in the year 2000.
The planned lay up of Unit 1 and last year's shutdown of Bruce Unit 2 would create a substantial surplus of heavy water, resulting in writedown costs of C$1.2 billion, he said.
Hydro is also reducing the scope of the Mattagami hydroelectric redevelopment project in northeastern Ontario to two 80-megawatt units at the Smoky Falls Generating Station.
Originally, Hydro had planned on 380 megawatts of new generation from the Mattagami River. This reduction in scope will result in a C$280 million write-off, Kupcis said.
He said the operating decisions will not affect current employee staffing levels.
Hydro's board also approved a charge of C$400 million in estimated future nuclear recovery expenditures against 1996 income.
"Nuclear accounts for more than 60 per cent of Hydro's generating supply and we will need improved performance if the utility is going to be successful in a competitive marketplace," Kupcis said.
The board also approved changes in some of Hydro's accounting policies which resulted in a C$400 million charge to 1996 operations.
